lessons.title: Population, migration and settlement
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Population, settlement, agriculture, industry, energy, transport, trade, tourism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate population density and natural increase
Explain causes and effects of migration
Describe settlement patterns, functions and urban problems
reviewNotes: Which regions are densely or sparsely populated, and the ranking of the two largest cities, should be verified. No population figures are quoted on purpose.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Population density** is the average number of people per square kilometre: total population ÷ area. **Birth rate** and **death rate** are the numbers of births and deaths per 1 000 people in a year. **Natural increase** = birth rate − death rate (per 1 000). If it is positive, the population grows.

blocks.caption: Push and pull factors in rural-urban migration
blocks.alt: Two boxes, rural area and town, joined by an arrow showing migration, with push and pull factors.

blocks.title: Distribution of population
blocks.md: People live where life is easier: fertile soil, reliable water, mild climate, flat land, jobs, trade routes and good services. They avoid steep mountains, dense forest, dry desert and swamps. In Cameroon the western highlands, the coast around Douala and the area around Yaoundé are densely populated, while the East and parts of the Adamawa plateau have fewer people per km².

**Migration** is the movement of people from one place to live in another. **Push factors** make people leave (unemployment, poor services, drought, conflict, floods). **Pull factors** attract them (jobs, schools, hospitals, electricity, safety). **Rural-urban migration** is very common in Cameroon. Effects: towns grow rapidly and may lack housing and jobs, while villages may lose young workers.

A **settlement** is a place where people live. Patterns: **nucleated** (houses grouped together), **dispersed** (scattered houses) and **linear** (along a road or river). Settlements have functions such as farming, market, administration, industry, port or tourism. **Site** is the exact land a settlement occupies; **situation** is its position in relation to other places.

blocks.title: Urban problems and solutions
blocks.md: Rapid growth can lead to overcrowding, slums, traffic jams, unemployment, pollution, waste and flooding. Solutions include planned housing, better public transport, waste collection, drainage, developing rural areas to reduce migration, and creating jobs.

blocks.title: Example 1: population density
blocks.statement: A district has 600 000 people and an area of 1 200 km². Calculate the population density.
steps: Density = population ÷ area.

blocks.title: Example 2: natural increase
blocks.statement: A country has a birth rate of 35 per 1 000 and a death rate of 10 per 1 000. Find the natural increase per 1 000 and say what happens to the population.
steps: Natural increase = 35 − 10.
The result is positive, so the population grows (by about 2.5% a year).

lessons.title: Agriculture in Cameroon and West/Central Africa
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Population, settlement, agriculture, industry, energy, transport, trade, tourism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Distinguish subsistence, commercial and plantation farming
Name the main food and cash crops and where they grow
Describe farming methods and the problems of farmers
reviewNotes: Crop-to-region links are given in general terms; a teacher should check them (esp. tea, rubber, Arabica/Robusta zones) against local sources.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: Agriculture is the main activity of many Cameroonians. **Subsistence farming** produces food mainly for the farmer's family (cassava, plantain, maize, yams, groundnuts, beans). **Commercial farming** produces crops for sale (cocoa, coffee, cotton). **Plantation farming** uses large estates, many workers and often processing on site (banana, oil palm, rubber, tea).

blocks.caption: Types of farming
blocks.alt: Three boxes labelled subsistence, commercial and plantation farming with example crops.

blocks.title: Crops and regions
blocks.md:
- Cocoa: forest zone of the Centre, South and Southwest.
- Coffee: Robusta in forest and coastal zones; Arabica in the western highlands.
- Cotton: savanna of the North and Far North.
- Banana, oil palm, rubber and tea: plantations around Mount Cameroon, Mungo and other humid, volcanic areas.
- Cattle and other livestock: Adamawa and North West grasslands.
- Fishing: the Atlantic coast and rivers and lakes.

Traditional methods include **shifting cultivation** (clearing a plot, farming it for a few years, then moving on), **bush fallowing**, **mixed cropping** and use of hoe and cutlass. Modern methods include fertilisers, improved seeds, irrigation, tractors and crop rotation. Mixed farming combines crops and livestock on one farm.

blocks.title: Problems of farmers
blocks.md:
- Poor roads, so crops rot before reaching the market.
- Pests and diseases; soil exhaustion.
- Falling or unstable prices of cash crops.
- Little credit and few modern inputs; land shortage in some areas.
- Climate risks: droughts in the north, floods in low areas.
Do not blame the weather alone in an exam answer: give human and economic causes as well.

blocks.title: Improving agriculture
blocks.md: Better roads and storage, training and extension workers, farmers' cooperatives, credit, improved seeds and fertilisers, processing crops locally to add value, irrigation in dry areas, and diversifying crops so that income does not depend on one product.

blocks.title: Example 1: classify
blocks.statement: Classify these farms: A) a family plot of cassava and plantain near Mbalmayo; B) a large banana estate with a packing station; C) a farmer who grows cocoa to sell to a buyer.
steps: A produces mainly for the family: subsistence.
B is a large estate with many workers and processing: plantation.
C grows a cash crop for sale: commercial farming.
blocks.answer: A subsistence, B plantation, C commercial.

blocks.title: Example 2: reasoning
blocks.statement: Why is cotton grown in the north of Cameroon and not in the equatorial forest?
steps: Cotton needs a wet season for growth and a dry season for harvest.
The north has a savanna climate with a dry season; the south has rain nearly all year.
Rain at harvest spoils the cotton, so the dry north suits it.
blocks.answer: Because the savanna climate gives a dry season for ripening and harvesting.

lessons.title: Industry and energy
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Population, settlement, agriculture, industry, energy, transport, trade, tourism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Classify economic activities as primary, secondary and tertiary
Explain factors affecting the location of industries
Describe the main sources of energy and their advantages
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: Edea aluminium plant and Sanaga dams (Song Loulou, Edea), Lagdo dam on the Benue, offshore oil and gas; and that hydro is the main source of electricity in Cameroon.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: Economic activities are grouped in three sectors. **Primary** activities take natural resources (farming, fishing, mining, logging). **Secondary** activities process or manufacture (food processing, brewing, cement, sawmills). **Tertiary** activities are services (trade, banking, transport, teaching, health, tourism).

blocks.caption: The three sectors of the economy
blocks.alt: Three boxes showing primary, secondary and tertiary activities with examples.

blocks.title: Location of industries
blocks.md: Industries are placed where costs are low and profit is high: **raw materials**, **power**, **labour**, **market**, **transport** (roads, railway, port), **capital** (money), **water** and **government policy**. Many industries in Cameroon are at Douala, which has the main port, a large market and good roads and rail. Edea, near the Sanaga, has an aluminium factory that uses hydroelectric power.

Energy sources are **non-renewable** (oil, natural gas, coal) because they will run out, or **renewable** (water, sun, wind, biomass), because they are replaced naturally. **Hydroelectric power** is the most important source of electricity in Cameroon, with dams on the Sanaga (Song Loulou, Edea) and the Benue (Lagdo). Oil and gas are produced offshore. Fuelwood is widely used for cooking.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
blocks.md:
- Hydro: renewable and cheap to run, but dams are expensive and depend on rainfall.
- Oil and gas: valuable exports, but pollute and may run out.
- Solar: clean and useful for remote villages, but depends on sunshine and has high set-up costs.
- Fuelwood: cheap, but causes deforestation.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Industry is not only factories: the tertiary sector is also an economic activity.
- 'Renewable' does not mean 'free of problems': dams change rivers and flood land.
- Always link a factory's location to at least two factors in your answer.

blocks.title: Example 1: classify
blocks.statement: Classify: A) cutting timber in the forest; B) sawing timber into planks at a mill in Douala; C) selling planks in a shop.
steps: Cutting timber takes a natural resource: primary.
Sawing is processing: secondary.
Selling is a service: tertiary.
blocks.answer: A primary, B secondary, C tertiary.

blocks.title: Example 2: location factors
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why an aluminium smelter is located at Edea.
steps: Smelting uses a great deal of electricity, so a nearby power source is vital.
Edea is near the Sanaga hydroelectric power and close to Douala port for importing materials and exporting aluminium.
The two main factors are power and transport.
blocks.answer: Hydroelectric power and good transport links.

lessons.title: Transport, trade and tourism
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Population, settlement, agriculture, industry, energy, transport, trade, tourism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Compare road, rail, air and water transport
Define imports, exports and the balance of trade
Describe tourism, its benefits and its problems in Cameroon
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the railway route, Kribi port, export/import lists (qualitative only), CEMAC and CFA franc description, and the list of attractions. The FCFA values in worked examples are invented for practice.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Transport** moves people and goods. **Roads** are the most widely used way in Cameroon and reach villages, but many are poor in the rainy season. **Railways** carry heavy goods and passengers over long distances: the main line runs from Douala through Yaoundé to Ngaoundéré. **Air transport** is fast and expensive. **Water transport** (ports at Douala, Kribi and Limbe; river transport on the Benue in the rainy season) is cheap for heavy goods.

blocks.caption: The railway line from Douala to Ngaoundéré (schematic)
blocks.alt: A line with four dots for Douala, Yaoundé, Belabo and Ngaoundéré.

blocks.title: Why transport matters
blocks.md: Good transport links bring markets to farmers, goods to shops, raw materials to factories and workers to jobs. They help national unity, attract industry and tourists, and allow help to reach people in emergencies. Poor transport raises prices and makes crops rot.

**Trade** is the buying and selling of goods and services. **Exports** are goods sold to other countries (for Cameroon: crude oil, cocoa, timber, banana, coffee, cotton, aluminium). **Imports** are goods bought from other countries (machinery, vehicles, fuel products, rice, wheat, medicines). The **balance of trade** is the value of exports minus the value of imports: a surplus if positive, a deficit if negative.

blocks.title: Regional trade
blocks.md: Cameroon belongs to the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), whose members share a common currency, the Central African CFA franc. Cameroon also trades with neighbours such as Nigeria and Chad. Regional groups aim to make trade easier by reducing barriers.

blocks.title: Tourism
blocks.md: Tourism brings income, jobs and foreign money, and encourages conservation. Attractions: Mount Cameroon, the beaches of Limbe and Kribi, Lobé falls, Waza National Park, the Dja and Korup reserves, Bafut and other palaces and festivals. Problems: poor roads and hotels, insecurity in some areas, pollution and damage to nature if it is not managed well.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Exports minus imports gives the balance of trade; do not reverse the order.
- A trade deficit is not the same as a loss for every business.
- Keep units and currency in answers (FCFA, billion FCFA).

blocks.title: Example 1: balance of trade
blocks.statement: In a year a country exports goods worth 800 billion FCFA and imports goods worth 950 billion FCFA. Calculate the balance of trade.
steps: Balance = exports − imports.
800 − 950 = −150 billion FCFA.
A negative result is a trade deficit.

blocks.title: Example 2: choose transport
blocks.statement: A trader must send 30 tonnes of cocoa from Yaoundé to the port of Douala. Which mode is best and why?
steps: The goods are heavy and not urgent.
Rail and road both link Yaoundé and Douala, and rail is cheaper for heavy bulk goods.
Air is far too costly for such a load.
blocks.answer: Rail (or road if rail is unavailable), because it is cheaper for heavy goods.
